# AI tools for writing — and verifying — code {#sec-ch-ai-tools}

> *"The hottest new programming language is English."* — Andrej Karpathy
> (January 2023). This chapter adds: *and the hottest new skill is reading
> code critically.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- explain, at a level sufficient to use them wisely, **how large language
  models generate code**: tokens, next-token probabilities, the softmax,
  temperature and sampling — with proofs of the key properties;
- describe the main families of tools — **chat assistants** (ChatGPT and
  similar), **AI-native editors** (Cursor), **IDE assistants** (GitHub Copilot
  in VS Code), **agents** — and what each is good at;
- explain how code models are **evaluated** (HumanEval, pass@$k$) and **prove**
  that the standard pass@$k$ estimator is unbiased;
- distinguish **vibe coding** from **structured prompt engineering**, and write
  structured prompts with requirements, context, interfaces and tests;
- **verify** AI-generated code systematically (reading, tests, static
  analysis, security and dependency checks), and know the documented risks.
:::

Cursor* · 14.3 *Code generation with Copilot in Visual Studio Code* ·

## Intuition: a very well-read, overconfident intern

An AI coding assistant is like an intern who has read **billions of lines** of
public code and documentation, types at superhuman speed, never gets tired —
and **does not know when it is wrong**. It produces code that *looks* right
because it has seen a lot of code that looks like it. Often the code *is*
right. Sometimes it calls a function that does not exist, mishandles an edge
case, or introduces a security hole, with exactly the same confident tone.

Used well, the intern multiplies your productivity. Used blindly, it
multiplies your bugs. The difference is **you**: the clarity of what you ask
(the *specification*) and the rigour with which you check what you get (the
*verification*). Everything in the previous thirteen chapters — types, edge
cases, invariants, exceptions, file formats, dependencies — is what lets you
do both.

## How a language model writes code {#sec-llm-basics}

The models behind these tools are **large language models** (LLMs) based on
the **Transformer** architecture [@vaswani2017], trained on enormous amounts of
text and code [@brown2020; @chen2021]. The details belong to later parts of
this book; here we need four ideas.

### Tokens

Text is split into **tokens** — frequent character sequences, produced by
algorithms such as **byte-pair encoding** (BPE) [@sennrich2016], which starts
from single bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a
new token. Common words and code fragments become single tokens (`def`,
` return`, ` self`); rare ones are split into pieces. A model's vocabulary $V$
typically has $10^4$–$10^5$ tokens.

### Next-token prediction

A language model defines a probability distribution over token sequences
$x_1,\dots,x_T$ by the **chain rule of probability**:
$$
P(x_1,\dots,x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} P(x_t \mid x_1,\dots,x_{t-1}).
$$ {#eq-chain-rule}

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## For the interested reader — proof of @eq-chain-rule
By the definition of conditional probability, $P(A\cap B) = P(A)\,P(B\mid A)$.
For $T = 1$ the formula is trivial. Assuming it for $T-1$:
$P(x_1..x_T) = P(x_1..x_{T-1})\,P(x_T\mid x_1..x_{T-1}) = \prod_{t=1}^{T-1}P(x_t\mid x_{<t})\cdot P(x_T\mid x_{<T})$.
$\blacksquare$ The formula is an identity: it holds for any distribution, which
is why a model only needs to learn the **conditional** next-token
distributions.
:::

So the model is a function that, given the **context** (the prompt plus what it
has generated so far), outputs a probability for every possible next token.
Generation repeats: pick a token, append it, ask again. Everything the model
"knows" about your project is what is in the context — which is why giving it
the right context matters so much (@sec-structured-prompting).

### Softmax and temperature

The network outputs a real **score** (*logit*) $z_i$ for each token $i$; the
**softmax** turns scores into probabilities. A **temperature** $\tau > 0$
controls how peaked the distribution is:
$$
p_i(\tau) = \frac{e^{z_i/\tau}}{\sum_{j\in V} e^{z_j/\tau}} .
$$ {#eq-softmax}

::: {#thm-softmax}
## Properties of the softmax with temperature
Let $z \in \mathbb{R}^{|V|}$.

1. $p_i(\tau) > 0$ and $\sum_i p_i(\tau) = 1$: it is a probability
   distribution.
2. **Shift invariance**: adding the same constant $c$ to every $z_i$ does not
   change $p(\tau)$.
3. If the maximum score is attained by a unique token $m$, then
   $p_m(\tau)\to 1$ as $\tau\to0^+$ (**greedy** decoding).
4. As $\tau\to\infty$, $p_i(\tau) \to 1/|V|$ for every $i$ (**uniform**
   distribution).
5. Larger scores get larger probabilities: $z_i > z_j \Rightarrow p_i > p_j$,
   and the ratio $p_i/p_j = e^{(z_i - z_j)/\tau}$ grows as $\tau$ decreases.
:::

*In one line:* low temperature makes the model pick its favourite token
(deterministic, repetitive); high temperature flattens the choice (diverse,
error-prone).

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## For the interested reader — proof of @thm-softmax
1. Exponentials are positive, and the numerators sum to the denominator.
2. $\dfrac{e^{(z_i + c)/\tau}}{\sum_j e^{(z_j+c)/\tau}} = \dfrac{e^{c/\tau}e^{z_i/\tau}}{e^{c/\tau}\sum_j e^{z_j/\tau}} = p_i(\tau)$.
3. By 2, subtract $z_m$: $p_m(\tau) = 1\big/\big(1 + \sum_{j\ne m} e^{(z_j - z_m)/\tau}\big)$.
   Each exponent $(z_j - z_m)/\tau \to -\infty$ because $z_j - z_m < 0$, so each
   term $\to 0$ and $p_m\to1$.
4. Each $z_i/\tau\to 0$, so each $e^{z_i/\tau}\to1$, numerator $\to 1$ and
   denominator $\to |V|$.
5. $p_i/p_j = e^{z_i/\tau}/e^{z_j/\tau} = e^{(z_i-z_j)/\tau}$, which is $>1$ when
   $z_i > z_j$ and is decreasing in $\tau$. $\blacksquare$

Property 2 is also how softmax is **computed** safely: subtract $\max_j z_j$
before exponentiating, so that no $e^{x}$ overflows (@sec-floats).
:::

```{python}
import numpy as np

def softmax(z, tau=1.0):
    z = np.asarray(z, dtype=float) / tau
    z = z - z.max()                      # shift invariance: avoids overflow in exp
    e = np.exp(z)
    return e / e.sum()

tokens = [" range", " enumerate", " zip", " sorted", " reversed"]
logits = [4.0, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0.0]      # hypothetical scores after "for i in"
for tau in [0.2, 0.7, 1.0, 2.0, 10.0]:
    p = softmax(logits, tau)
    print(f"tau={tau:>4}: " + "  ".join(f"{t.strip()}={q:.2f}" for t, q in zip(tokens, p)))
print(softmax([1000, 999]), "(no overflow thanks to the shift)")
```

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tauSlider = Inputs.range([0.1, 5], {step: 0.05, value: 1, label: "temperature τ"})
softmaxData = {
  const toks = ["range", "enumerate", "zip", "sorted", "reversed"];
  const z = [4.0, 2.5, 1.5, 0.5, 0.0];
  const m = Math.max(...z);
  const e = z.map(v => Math.exp((v - m) / tauSlider));
  const s = e.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  return toks.map((t, i) => ({token: t, p: e[i] / s}));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| label: fig-softmax-temperature
//| fig-cap: "Next-token probabilities for the same scores at different temperatures (hypothetical logits after the prompt `for i in`)."
Plot.plot({y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "probability"}, x: {label: null, domain: ["range", "enumerate", "zip", "sorted", "reversed"]},
  marks: [Plot.barY(softmaxData, {x: "token", y: "p", fill: "steelblue"}),
          Plot.text(softmaxData, {x: "token", y: "p", text: d => d.p.toFixed(2), dy: -8}), Plot.ruleY([0])]})
```
:::

Two common refinements: **top-$k$ sampling** keeps only the $k$ most probable
tokens; **nucleus (top-$p$) sampling** keeps the smallest set of tokens whose
probabilities sum to at least $p$ [@holtzman2020]. For code, assistants
usually run at low temperature: code tolerates little creativity at the token
level.

### What follows for you

- The model optimises **plausibility**, not **correctness**. A wrong but
  common-looking line can have high probability.
- Its knowledge has a **cut-off date** and reflects the frequency of patterns
  in training data: recent library versions, rare APIs and your private code
  are poorly represented unless you put them in the context.
- It has **no access to the truth** unless a tool gives it one: running the
  code, reading the documentation, executing the tests. Modern agentic tools do
  exactly that — and that is why they work better.
- By @thm-halting and Rice's theorem (@sec-halting), no tool — AI or not — can
  decide in general that a program is correct. Verification remains an
  engineering activity.

## The tools {#sec-ai-tools-landscape}

The landscape changes every few months; what follows describes the **kinds**
of tools covered in the course, as of the writing of this book.

| Kind | Examples | How you use it | Strengths | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Chat assistant** | ChatGPT (OpenAI, launched November 2022), Claude, Gemini | describe a task in a conversation, paste code and errors | explaining concepts and errors, drafting functions, reviewing a snippet, brainstorming designs | it sees only what you paste; copy–paste errors; outdated APIs |
| **IDE assistant** | GitHub Copilot in VS Code (2021, originally powered by Codex [@chen2021]) | inline completions as you type; a chat panel aware of open files; "edit" and agent modes | low friction, boilerplate, tests, small refactors | accepting completions without reading them |
| **AI-native editor** | Cursor (a VS Code-based editor by Anysphere) | the editor indexes the whole codebase; chat and multi-file edits ("composer"/agent) with diffs to accept or reject | changes spanning many files, codebase questions | large diffs are hard to review; scope creep |
| **Coding agents** | agentic modes of the above; command-line agents | give a goal; the agent plans, edits files, runs commands and tests, iterates | multi-step tasks with a feedback loop | give it tests and limits; review everything; protect secrets |

: Families of AI coding tools {#tbl-ai-tools}

### ChatGPT-style assistants: a workflow

1. **State the task and constraints** (see the template in
   @sec-structured-prompting).
2. **Paste the relevant code** and the **exact error message** with its
   traceback (@sec-anatomy) — not a paraphrase.
3. Ask for an **explanation** as well as the code; ask what could go wrong.
4. **Run** the answer, **test** it, and paste back the *actual* behaviour if
   it fails.
5. Never paste secrets, personal data or proprietary code you are not allowed
   to share (the phone book's company values data protection: real contacts
   are personal data under GDPR).

### Copilot in VS Code: a workflow

- Write a **descriptive function signature and docstring** first
  (@sec-docstrings-functions); completions follow it. Type hints help.
- Treat a grey suggestion as a **proposal**: read it before pressing
  <kbd>Tab</kbd>.
- Use the chat to **generate tests** for the function you wrote, then make them
  pass — the reverse of the usual direction, and much safer.

### Cursor: a workflow

- Ask questions **about the codebase** ("where is the JSON file written?") —
  answers point to files you can open.
- For multi-file changes, describe the change, then **review the diff file by
  file**; reject what you do not understand.
- Keep a project **rules file** describing conventions (style, libraries,
  "never use print for errors"), so they are part of every context.

### What the evidence says

- In a randomised controlled trial, developers with Copilot implemented a
  small HTTP server **55.8% faster** than the control group [@peng2023]. The
  task was small and self-contained.
- In another randomised trial on **real issues** in large, mature open-source
  projects they knew well, experienced developers using early-2025 tools took
  **19% longer** — while believing they had been about 20% faster
  [@becker2025].
- Of 1,689 programs Copilot generated for security-relevant scenarios, about
  **40% were vulnerable** [@pearce2022].
- Across 16 models and 576,000 generated samples, on average at least **5.2%**
  (commercial models) and **21.7%** (open-source models) of recommended
  packages **did not exist** — names an attacker can register
  [@spracklen2025] (@sec-choosing-packages).

The picture is consistent: large gains on well-specified, self-contained tasks;
smaller or negative gains when the context is large and implicit; real
security and supply-chain risks when output is not verified.

## Measuring code models: pass@$k$ {#sec-passk}

How do we measure whether a model writes correct code? The Codex paper
introduced **HumanEval**: 164 hand-written Python problems, each with a
signature, a docstring and hidden **unit tests**; a generated solution counts
as correct if it passes all the tests [@chen2021]. Since generation is random,
one reports **pass@$k$**: the probability that **at least one of $k$**
generated samples passes.

If each sample is independently correct with probability $p$, then
$$
\text{pass@}k = 1 - (1-p)^k ,
$$ {#eq-passk}
because "none of $k$ is correct" has probability $(1-p)^k$ (independence) and
we take the complement. With $p = 0.3$: pass@1 $= 0.3$, pass@10
$= 1 - 0.7^{10} \approx 0.97$ — sampling several solutions and **testing** them
is very effective, which is precisely why tests are so valuable when working
with AI.

In practice $p$ is unknown. Chen et al. generate $n \ge k$ samples per
problem, count the $c$ correct ones, and use the estimator
$$
\widehat{\text{pass@}k} = 1 - \frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom nk}.
$$ {#eq-passk-estimator}

::: {#thm-passk-unbiased}
## The pass@$k$ estimator is unbiased
If the $n$ samples are independent and each is correct with probability $p$,
then $\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{\text{pass@}k}\big] = 1 - (1-p)^k$.
:::

*In one line:* the fraction $\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom nk$ is the probability that
$k$ samples chosen at random among the $n$ are all wrong; averaging over the
randomness of the $n$ samples gives the probability that $k$ fresh samples are
all wrong.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## For the interested reader — proof of @thm-passk-unbiased
Generate the $n$ samples, and independently choose a subset $S$ of $k$ of
them uniformly at random. Compute the probability $q$ that all samples in $S$
are wrong in two ways.

*Conditioning on the samples.* Given the $n$ samples with $c$ correct ones,
there are $\binom nk$ equally likely subsets, of which $\binom{n-c}{k}$
contain only wrong samples (@thm-comb). So
$q = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom nk\right]$.

*Directly.* Because $S$ is chosen independently of the outcomes and the
samples are i.i.d., the $k$ samples in $S$ are themselves $k$ independent
samples, each wrong with probability $1-p$. So $q = (1-p)^k$.

Equating, $\mathbb{E}\big[\binom{n-c}{k}/\binom nk\big] = (1-p)^k$, and by
linearity of expectation
$\mathbb{E}\big[\widehat{\text{pass@}k}\big] = 1 - (1-p)^k$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The "obvious" plug-in estimate $1 - (1 - c/n)^k$ is **biased** (it
underestimates), because $x\mapsto 1-(1-x)^k$ is concave (Jensen's
inequality). For computation, the binomial coefficients can be huge; Chen et
al. use the equivalent product
$$
\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom nk} = \prod_{i=n-c+1}^{n}\Big(1 - \frac ki\Big),
$$
which follows by writing both coefficients with factorials:
$\frac{(n-c)!\,(n-k)!}{n!\,(n-c-k)!} = \prod_{i=n-c+1}^{n}\frac{i-k}{i}$
(for $n - c \ge k$; otherwise the ratio is $0$ and the estimate is $1$).

```{python}
from math import comb, prod
import random

def pass_at_k(n: int, c: int, k: int) -> float:
    """Unbiased pass@k estimator of Chen et al. (2021), numerically stable form."""
    if n - c < k:
        return 1.0
    return 1.0 - prod(1 - k / i for i in range(n - c + 1, n + 1))

print(pass_at_k(20, 5, 1), pass_at_k(20, 5, 10), 1 - comb(15, 10) / comb(20, 10))

# Monte Carlo check of unbiasedness (and of the bias of the plug-in estimate)
random.seed(0)
p, n, k, trials = 0.15, 20, 5, 20_000
unbiased = plugin = 0.0
for _ in range(trials):
    c = sum(random.random() < p for _ in range(n))
    unbiased += pass_at_k(n, c, k)
    plugin += 1 - (1 - c / n) ** k
print(f"true {1 - (1 - p) ** k:.4f} | unbiased {unbiased / trials:.4f} | plug-in {plugin / trials:.4f}")
```

## Vibe coding versus structured prompt engineering {#sec-vibe-vs-structured}

### Vibe coding

In February 2025 Andrej Karpathy described a new way of programming he called
**vibe coding**: you *"fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and
forget that the code even exists"* [@karpathy2025] — you describe what you
want, accept the changes without reading them, paste error messages back, and
keep going until it seems to work. The term spread instantly (Collins
Dictionary named it its 2025 word of the year).

Vibe coding has a legitimate niche: **throwaway prototypes**, personal
scripts, exploring an idea, learning what is possible. Its defining feature —
*not reading the code* — is also its limit: nobody understands the result, so
nobody can guarantee its correctness, security or maintainability, and every
change risks breaking something invisible. For anything that handles real
users' data, money or safety, or that must live longer than a weekend, it is
not engineering.

### Structured prompt engineering {#sec-structured-prompting}

**Structured prompt engineering** treats the prompt as a **specification** and
the output as a **proposal to be verified**. A good code prompt contains:

| Part | What to write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Goal** | one sentence: what the code must achieve | anchors everything else |
| **Context** | language/version, libraries and versions, relevant existing code, conventions | the model only knows what is in the context |
| **Interface** | function/class signatures, types, inputs and outputs | constrains the solution; makes it testable |
| **Requirements** | functional behaviour, including **edge cases** and **error handling** | the parts the model is most likely to skip |
| **Constraints** | what *not* to do: no new dependencies, no I/O in domain code, performance limits | prevents plausible-but-unwanted designs |
| **Examples / tests** | input → expected output pairs, or a test suite to pass | the single most effective addition: examples steer the model [@brown2020], tests let you verify |
| **Output format** | "return only the function", "explain the design first", "show a diff" | makes the answer usable and reviewable |

Asking the model to **reason step by step** or to **explain its plan before
writing code** tends to improve results on complex tasks (*chain-of-thought*
prompting [@wei2022]). Iterate: when the result is wrong, refine the
specification or add the failing test, rather than just saying "it doesn't
work".

::: {#exm-structured-prompt}
## A structured prompt for the project
```text
GOAL: Write a function that normalises phone numbers for a terminal phone book.

CONTEXT: Python 3.13, standard library only. Numbers are typed by Italian users;
the result is stored as a string in a JSON file.

INTERFACE:
    def normalize_phone(text: str, default_cc: str = "39") -> str

REQUIREMENTS:
1. Ignore spaces, '-', '.', '(' and ')'.
2. A leading '+' or '00' introduces the country code; otherwise prepend default_cc.
3. KEEP leading zeros of the national number (Italian landlines start with 0).
4. Return '+' followed by digits only (E.164 style), 8 to 15 digits in total.
5. Raise ValueError with a clear message for any other character or wrong length.

CONSTRAINTS: no regex libraries beyond `re`; no int() conversion of the number.

TESTS (must all pass):
    "06 1234 5678"      -> "+390612345678"
    "+39 333-123.4567"  -> "+393331234567"
    "0039 333 1234567"  -> "+393331234567"
    "(02) 1234567"      -> "+39021234567"
    "12ab34"            -> ValueError
    "+1 2"              -> ValueError

OUTPUT: the function with a docstring, then a list of edge cases you considered.
```
:::

## Verifying AI-generated code {#sec-verification}

Here is a **plausible** answer to a vaguer prompt ("write a function that
normalises Italian phone numbers"), of the kind assistants frequently produce
— short, readable, and wrong:

```{python}
def normalize_phone_v1(text, default_cc="39"):
    digits = "".join(ch for ch in text if ch.isdigit())
    if text.strip().startswith("+"):
        return "+" + digits
    return "+" + default_cc + str(int(digits))
```

The tests from the structured prompt expose it immediately:

```{python}
TESTS = [
    ("06 1234 5678", "+390612345678"),
    ("+39 333-123.4567", "+393331234567"),
    ("0039 333 1234567", "+393331234567"),
    ("(02) 1234567", "+39021234567"),
    ("12ab34", ValueError),
    ("+1 2", ValueError),
]

def run_tests(fn):
    failures = 0
    for text, expected in TESTS:
        try:
            got = fn(text)
        except Exception as err:
            got = type(err)
        ok = got == expected
        failures += not ok
        print(f"{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}  {text!r:22} expected {expected!s:<26} got {got}")
    print(f"--> {len(TESTS) - failures}/{len(TESTS)} passed\n")

run_tests(normalize_phone_v1)
```

Only one test out of six passes, and each failure is a lesson from earlier
chapters: `int()` **drops leading
zeros** (@sec-casting); the `00` prefix is treated as part of the number;
letters are **silently ignored** instead of rejected (validate input,
@sec-ch-exceptions); no length check (E.164 [@itue164]). A corrected version,
written against the specification:

```{python}
import re

ALLOWED_SEPARATORS = " -.()"

def normalize_phone(text: str, default_cc: str = "39") -> str:
    """Normalise a phone number to '+<digits>' (E.164 style).

    Separators ' -.()' are ignored; a leading '+' or '00' introduces the country
    code, otherwise `default_cc` is prepended. Leading zeros are kept.
    Raises ValueError for invalid characters or a total length outside 8..15 digits.
    """
    s = "".join(ch for ch in text.strip() if ch not in ALLOWED_SEPARATORS)
    if s.startswith("+"):
        body = s[1:]
    elif s.startswith("00"):
        body = s[2:]
    else:
        body = default_cc + s
    if not re.fullmatch(r"\d+", body):
        raise ValueError(f"invalid characters in phone number: {text!r}")
    if not 8 <= len(body) <= 15:
        raise ValueError(f"phone number must have 8-15 digits, got {len(body)}: {text!r}")
    return "+" + body

run_tests(normalize_phone)
```

### A verification checklist

1. **Read every line.** If you cannot explain a line, you cannot ship it. Ask
   the assistant to explain it — then check the explanation against the
   documentation.
2. **Run it**, on normal inputs *and* on edge cases: empty input, zero,
   negative numbers, huge inputs, Unicode, missing files, wrong types.
3. **Test it**: write (or generate, then review) unit tests *before* accepting
   the code; keep them in the project (`doctest`, `unittest`, `pytest`).
   Property-based testing (e.g. the Hypothesis library) generates hundreds of
   random inputs to check invariants such as "normalising twice gives the same
   result".
4. **Check the invariants and contracts** you know from the design (class
   invariants, @sec-encapsulation; loop invariants, @sec-loop-invariants) —
   add `assert`s for internal ones.
5. **Static analysis**: a linter (`ruff`), a type checker (`mypy`), a security
   scanner (`bandit`), a secrets scanner. They catch whole classes of errors for
   free.
6. **Dependencies**: does every imported package **exist**, is it the one you
   think, is it maintained, is its licence acceptable (@sec-choosing-packages)?
7. **Security and privacy**: no hard-coded secrets, no `eval` on user input,
   no SQL built by string concatenation, no personal data sent to external
   services without permission.
8. **Review the diff, not just the result**: in multi-file edits, unrelated
   changes slip in.

::: {.callout-important}
## The rule of this book
Use AI tools as much as you like to **draft**, **explain**, **review** and
**test** — but you are the engineer of record: **never commit code you have not
read, understood and verified.**
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** The brief closes with *"if you have doubts about how to
set up the classes, write to me before starting"* — today you could also ask an
assistant, and this chapter shows how to do it well: give it the brief as a
**structured prompt** (requirements, constraints such as "keep the interaction
logic out of the domain classes", the JSON format), ask for a **design and its
rationale** before any code, then use it to **generate edge-case tests** for
your own implementation (empty file, duplicate contact, non-numeric choice,
interrupted save). The phone-number normaliser above is a ready-made
improvement for the project's `Contatto`, which stores numbers as `int` and
therefore loses leading zeros (@sec-ch-project-phonebook).
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Accepting code you have not read** (the essence of vibe coding).
- **Vague prompts** → plausible code for a different problem.
- **Missing context**: library versions, existing code, conventions.
- **Hallucinated APIs and packages**: check names against the official
  documentation and PyPI.
- **Pasting secrets or personal data** into external tools.
- **Letting the model grade itself**: "are you sure?" is not verification;
  tests are.
- **Over-reliance while learning**: if the assistant writes all your exercises,
  you do not learn to program — and you lose the very skill needed to verify
  it. Do the exercises of this book by hand first.
:::

## Summary

- LLMs generate code token by token from conditional probabilities (chain
  rule); the softmax with temperature turns scores into probabilities —
  low $\tau$ is greedy, high $\tau$ uniform.
- They optimise plausibility, not correctness, and know only what is in their
  training data and context.
- Chat assistants, IDE assistants (Copilot), AI-native editors (Cursor) and
  agents differ in how much context they see and how much they act.
- Code models are evaluated with unit tests and pass@$k$; the estimator
  $1 - \binom{n-c}{k}/\binom nk$ is unbiased.
- Vibe coding is fine for throwaway prototypes; engineering requires
  structured prompts (goal, context, interface, requirements, constraints,
  tests, format) and systematic verification.
- Evidence: big speed-ups on small, well-specified tasks; slow-downs on large
  familiar codebases; frequent security flaws and hallucinated packages when
  unverified.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-ch14-softmax}
For logits $z = (2, 1, 0)$ compute the softmax probabilities by hand (with
$e \approx 2.718$) at $\tau = 1$, and the ratio $p_1/p_3$ at $\tau = 1$ and
$\tau = 0.5$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$e^2 \approx 7.389$, $e^1\approx 2.718$, $e^0 = 1$; sum $\approx 11.107$:
$p \approx (0.665, 0.245, 0.090)$. $p_1/p_3 = e^{2/\tau}$: $e^2\approx 7.39$ at
$\tau=1$, $e^4 \approx 54.6$ at $\tau = 0.5$.
:::

::: {#exr-ch14-passk}
A model solves a problem with probability $p = 0.2$ per sample. How many
samples $k$ are needed for pass@$k \ge 0.9$? If you can run a test suite on
each sample, what does this suggest about how to use such a model?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$1 - 0.8^k \ge 0.9 \iff 0.8^k\le 0.1 \iff k \ge \ln 0.1/\ln 0.8 \approx 10.3$,
so $k = 11$. With automatic tests, generating several candidates and keeping
one that passes turns a weak per-sample accuracy into a high success rate —
provided the tests are good (a wrong test selects wrong code).
:::

::: {#exr-ch14-prompt}
Write a structured prompt (goal, context, interface, requirements,
constraints, tests, output) asking an assistant for the `load_contacts`
function of @exr-ch8-load. Then compare what you get with the solution of that
exercise and list the differences.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Key requirements to state: return `[]` for a missing **or empty** file; raise a
custom, chained error for invalid JSON; open with `encoding="utf-8"`; no
`os.path.exists` check (TOCTOU, @exm-toctou); tests for the three cases.
Typical differences in generated code: an LBYL existence check, empty files not
handled (`JSONDecodeError`), a bare `except`, missing encoding.
:::

::: {#exr-ch14-idempotent}
Write a test that checks the **idempotence** of `normalize_phone`
(normalising an already-normalised number returns it unchanged) on the valid
test inputs. Why is idempotence a good property to test?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```python
for text, expected in TESTS:
    if expected is not ValueError:
        once = normalize_phone(text)
        assert normalize_phone(once) == once
```
Stored numbers may be normalised again (on load, on edit); idempotence
guarantees that repeated processing never corrupts them. Properties like this
are ideal for property-based testing because they hold for *all* valid inputs.
:::

## Further reading {.unnumbered}

- @chen2021 — the Codex paper: HumanEval, pass@$k$ and its estimator
  (Section 2.1), and an early discussion of risks.
- @vaswani2017 — the Transformer; @brown2020 — few-shot prompting in GPT-3;
  @wei2022 — chain-of-thought prompting; @holtzman2020 — nucleus sampling;
  @sennrich2016 — byte-pair encoding. All will be studied in depth in the
  generative-AI part of the book.
- @peng2023 and @becker2025 — two randomised trials with different settings
  and opposite results: read both.
- @pearce2022 — security of AI-generated code; @spracklen2025 — package
  hallucinations.
- The official documentation of the tools (GitHub Copilot, Cursor, ChatGPT):
  features change quickly, so always check the current version.
